## Part1

Reading in Data (question 1)

```{r}
beandata <- read_xlsx("C:\\Users\\lbmoy2\\Downloads\\lbmoy2_beans.xlsx")

```

The data has been read into the object `beandata`. This object is a `r typeof(beandata)` that has `r length(beandata[1,])` variables and `r length(beandata[,1])` observations.


Modifying beandata by filtering (obs and vars), simplifying var names, and adding new summary variables (question 2)

```{r}
modbean <- beandata %>%
             select(-c(Eccentricity, Solidity)) %>%
               rename("LengthMaj" = MajorAxisLength, "LengthMin" = MinorAxisLength) %>%
                 filter(Class %in% c("CALI", "HOROZ", "SEKER", "SIRA", "DERMASON")) %>%
                   mutate("AvgMaj" = mean(LengthMaj), "AvgMin" = mean(LengthMin) ) %>%
                     mutate("PerimCate" = if_else(Perimeter > 804.048, "Largest", if_else(Perimeter > 706.901, "Medium", "Lowest"))) %>%
                       arrange(desc(Extent))

print(as_tibble(modbean))
```




Making 2-way Contingency table (question 3)

```{r}
modbean %>% 
  filter(LengthMaj < 404.4919)

table(modbean$Class, modbean$PerimCate) 



```
The top left number is the number of cali beans that have the largest perimeter.


Numeric Summary (question 4)
```{r}
modbean %>%
  group_by(Class) %>%
    summarize(AvgAr = mean(Area), AvgPer = mean(Perimeter),  MinAr = min(Area), MinPer = min(Perimeter) ,
            SkewAr = skewness(Area), SkewPer = skewness(Perimeter) , VarAr = var(Area), AvgPer = var(Perimeter))

```
The cali bean has an avg area of 75519.73, avg perimeter of 4730.073, a min area of 45666 and min perimeter of 789.770.
Its skewness of the area is 0.44478747 and the skewness of the perimeter is 0.1495999 (both are more positively skewed). The variance is 91721871.


## Part2

URL : https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/42/glass+identification

Why it interests me: I just picked this out because it said glass and I think reflections are cool. The contents don't interest me too much, nor do I know why this data is important.

Reading in Data
```{r}
glassdata <- read_csv("C:\\Users\\lbmoy2\\Downloads\\glass+identification\\glass.data", col_names = FALSE, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename("Id" = X1,
         "Refrac_index" = X2,
         "Sodium" = X3,
         "Magnesium" = X4,
         "Aluminum" = X5,
         "Silicon" = X6,
         "Potassium" = X7,
         "Calcium" = X8,
         "Barium" = X9,
         "Iron" = X10,
         "Type_of_glass" = X11)
```

Two questions (that can be answered)
1) What is the max refraction index?

2) How do the averages of elements compare to one another?

Summary Stats and Tables
```{r}
glassdata %>%
  group_by(Type_of_glass) %>%
    summarize( max = max(Refrac_index))
glassdata %>%
  summarize(smean = mean(Sodium), mmean = mean(Magnesium),amean = mean(Aluminum),simean = mean(Silicon),pmean = mean(Potassium),cmean = mean(Calcium),bmean = mean(Barium),imean = mean(Iron))

```

1)Max Refraction Index is from type 2 glass with 1.534
2) Silicon is obviously has the highest concentration in glass and the next is sodium.
